ladder.title: The greedy Egyptian fraction algorithm terminates
ladder.q:
Let $0<\frac ab<1$ with $a,b$ positive integers. Let $n_1$ be the least positive integer with $\frac1{n_1}\le\frac ab$, replace $\frac ab$ by $\frac ab-\frac1{n_1}$, and repeat while the remainder is nonzero.

Prove that this process stops after at most $a$ steps, and that the denominators it produces are distinct, so that every rational number in $(0,1)$ is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions.
ladder.source: Fibonacci, Liber Abaci (1202); J. J. Sylvester, On a point in the theory of vulgar fractions, Amer. J. Math. 3 (1880), 332-335
ladder.note: The basic existence statement behind every question on the concept: representations always exist, so the problems are about their length, size and location.

ladder.title: Prime powers are never the largest denominator
ladder.q:
Suppose $1=\frac1{m_1}+\cdots+\frac1{m_k}$ with integers $1\le m_1<\cdots<m_k$ and $k\ge2$.

Prove that $m_k$ is not a prime power: if $p$ is a prime and $a\ge1$, then $m_k\neq p^a$.
ladder.source: Folklore; recorded as an easy remark at erdosproblems.com/292
ladder.note: A p-adic valuation argument that already shows the set of possible largest denominators misses infinitely many integers; the research question asks how large that exceptional set is.

ladder.title: Erdős–Straus outside one residue class mod 24
ladder.q:
Let $n>2$ be an integer with $n\not\equiv 1 \pmod{24}$.

Prove that there exist integers $1\le x<y<z$ with $$\frac4n=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z.$$
ladder.source: Consequence of Mordell's parametric identities (L. J. Mordell, Diophantine Equations, Academic Press, 1969): every prime outside the classes 1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529 mod 840 has a solution, and all of these classes are 1 mod 24; see erdosproblems.com/242 and C. Pomerance's survey notes
ladder.note: Explicit identities settle all but one residue class mod 24; this is why the conjecture is really about primes $p\equiv1 \pmod{24}$.

ladder.title: A lower bound for the largest denominator in a representation of 1
ladder.q:
For $k\ge1$ let $f(k)$ be the least possible value of $n_k$ over all integers $1\le n_1<\cdots<n_k$ with $\frac1{n_1}+\cdots+\frac1{n_k}=1$.

Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $k_0$ such that $f(k)\ge\left(\frac{e}{e-1}-\varepsilon\right)k$ for all $k\ge k_0$.
ladder.source: Trivial direction recorded at erdosproblems.com/285 (problem from P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory, 1980)
ladder.note: Comparing with $\sum_{N/e<n\le N}1/n\approx1$ gives the lower bound; the research problems ask that it be sharp, i.e. that $k$ denominators can be packed into an interval of width $(e-1+o(1))k$.

ladder.title: A large set with no subset of reciprocal sum 1
ladder.q: Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$ there is a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\ge\left(1-\frac1e-\varepsilon\right)N$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\neq1$ for every nonempty $S\subseteq A$.
ladder.source: Folklore; stated as the trivial lower bound in Erdős Problem 300 and in Y. P. Liu and M. Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113 (2024)
ladder.note: An interval of integers whose reciprocals sum to slightly less than 1 gives the extremal example; the hard direction (rung below) shows no denser set works.

ladder.title: Erdős–Straus holds for almost all n
ladder.q:
For $N\ge2$ let $E(N)$ be the number of integers $2\le n\le N$ for which the equation $\frac4n=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z$ has no solution in positive integers $x,y,z$.

Prove that there is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $$E(N)\ll N\exp\!\left(-c(\log N)^{2/3}\right).$$
ladder.source: R. C. Vaughan, On a problem of Erdős, Straus and Schinzel, Mathematika 17 (1970), 193-198
ladder.note: Combining many parametric families with a sieve shows the exceptional set is very thin; the open problem asks that it be empty.

ladder.title: Almost every integer is the largest denominator of a representation of 1
ladder.q:
Let $A$ be the set of positive integers $n$ for which there exist integers $1\le m_1<\cdots<m_k=n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{m_i}=1$, and let $B=\mathbb N\setminus A$.

Prove that for all sufficiently large $x$ $$\#\{n\le x: n\in B\}\asymp\frac{x\log\log x}{\log x}.$$ In particular $A$ has natural density $1$.
ladder.source: G. Martin, Denser Egyptian fractions, Acta Arith. 95 (2000), no. 3; arXiv:math/9811112
ladder.note: Upgrades the prime-power obstruction rung to the true order of the exceptional set; the same paper determines the minimal largest denominator for $t$-term representations.

ladder.title: Croot's colouring theorem
ladder.q: Prove that for every integer $r\ge1$ there is an integer $N(r)$ with the following property: whenever $\{2,3,\ldots,N(r)\}$ is coloured with $r$ colours, there is a set $S$ of integers, all of the same colour, with $$\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1.$$
ladder.source: E. S. Croot III, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. of Math. (2) 157 (2003), no. 2, 545-556
ladder.note: Answers the Erdős–Graham colouring question; its method (finding many smooth denominators in one colour class) is the starting point for the density versions below.

ladder.title: Bloom's density theorem for unit fractions
ladder.q:
(a) Prove that there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $$\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ge C\,\frac{\log\log\log N}{\log\log N}\,\log N$$ contains a finite $S\subseteq A$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.

(b) Prove that every $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ of positive upper density contains a finite $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.
ladder.source: T. F. Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions, arXiv:2112.03726 (2021)
ladder.note: Turns Croot's colouring method into a density result via a Fourier-analytic argument; a set with bounded gaps has positive density, and a stronger technical form of the theorem gives $(1-o(1))\log N$ disjoint representations of 1 inside $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

ladder.title: Liu–Sawhney: the sharp density threshold 1 - 1/e
ladder.q:
(a) Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n\ge(\log N)^{4/5+\varepsilon}$ contains a subset $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.

(b) Prove that for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac12)$ and all sufficiently large $N$, every $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\ge\left(1-\frac1e+\varepsilon\right)N$ contains a subset $S$ with $\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=1$.
ladder.source: Y. P. Liu and M. Sawhney, On further questions regarding unit fractions, arXiv:2404.07113 (2024), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3
ladder.note: Part (b) matches the construction of the earlier rung, so the maximal size of a set with no subset of reciprocal sum 1 is $(1-1/e+o(1))N$; the same paper's refined method also treats denominators of $a/b$ and the quantity $t(N)$.

ladder.title: A covering system with distinct moduli
ladder.q:
(a) Prove that every integer satisfies at least one of the congruences $$x\equiv0\pmod2,\quad x\equiv0\pmod3,\quad x\equiv1\pmod4,\quad x\equiv5\pmod6,\quad x\equiv7\pmod{12}.$$

(b) Prove that if the congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le k$, cover every integer, then $\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{n_i}\ge1$, with equality if and only if every integer satisfies exactly one of them.
ladder.source: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950), 113-123
ladder.note: Erdős's original example and the density count used in every later argument about coverings.

ladder.title: Why 2^r consecutive integers are needed
ladder.q: Let $r\ge1$. Show that the $r$ congruences $x\equiv2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$, $1\le i\le r$, cover each of the $2^r-1$ consecutive integers $1,2,\ldots,2^r-1$ but do not cover all integers.
ladder.source: Folklore; given as the sharpness example in Erdős Problem 275
ladder.note: Shows the threshold $2^r$ in the Crittenden–Vanden Eynden theorem cannot be lowered.

ladder.title: A Sierpiński number from a covering
ladder.q:
(a) Prove that for every integer $n\ge0$ the number $78557\cdot2^n+1$ is divisible by at least one of the primes $3,5,7,13,19,37,73$, and hence is composite.

(b) Deduce, using the Chinese remainder theorem, that there are infinitely many odd $k$ for which $k\cdot2^n+1$ is composite for every $n\ge0$.
ladder.source: W. Sierpiński, Sur un problème concernant les nombres k·2^n+1, Elem. Math. 15 (1960), 73-74 (infinitely many such k); the example 78557 is due to J. Selfridge (1962, unpublished)
ladder.note: Each prime $p$ in the set handles one residue class of $n$ modulo the order of 2 mod $p$, so a covering system becomes a covering set; the research problems ask whether every such phenomenon must come from a covering.

ladder.title: No exact covering with distinct moduli
ladder.q:
Let $k\ge2$ and let $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le k$, be congruences with $1<n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_k$.

Prove that some integer satisfies none or at least two of these congruences. In fact, prove more: in any partition of $\mathbb Z$ into $k\ge2$ residue classes, the largest modulus occurs at least twice.
ladder.source: Mirsky and Newman, and independently Davenport and Rado (unpublished); reported in P. Erdős, On a problem concerning congruence systems, Mat. Lapok 3 (1952), 122-128
ladder.note: The generating-function proof uses $\sum_i z^{a_i}/(1-z^{n_i})=1/(1-z)$ and looks at a primitive $n_k$-th root of unity; this is the case $G=\mathbb Z$ of the coset-partition question.

ladder.title: r congruences covering 2^r consecutive integers cover everything
ladder.q: Let $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$, $1\le i\le r$, be $r$ congruences (the moduli need not be distinct). Prove that if every one of the integers $1,2,\ldots,2^r$ satisfies at least one of them, then every integer satisfies at least one of them.
ladder.source: R. B. Crittenden and C. L. Vanden Eynden, Any n arithmetic progressions covering the first 2^n integers cover all integers, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 24 (1970), 475–481
ladder.note: Together with the sharpness rung on 2^r consecutive integers this settles Erdős Problem 275 exactly.

ladder.title: Hough: the minimum modulus is bounded
ladder.q:
Call a finite set of congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with distinct moduli $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ a distinct covering system if every integer satisfies at least one of them.

Prove that every distinct covering system has $n_1\le10^{16}$.
ladder.source: R. Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. of Math. (2) 181 (2015), no. 1, 361-382
ladder.note: Answers Erdős's minimum modulus problem negatively using a probabilistic sieve with the Lovász local lemma.

ladder.title: The distortion method: Schinzel's question and a smaller minimum modulus
ladder.q:
(a) Prove that every distinct covering system has least modulus less than $10^6$.

(b) Prove that in every finite covering of $\mathbb Z$ by congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with all $n_i>1$, there are $i\neq j$ with $n_i\mid n_j$.
ladder.source: P. Balister, B. Bollobás, R. Morris, J. Sahasrabudhe and M. Tiba, On the Erdős covering problem: the density of the uncovered set, Invent. Math. 228 (2022), no. 1, 377-414; arXiv:1811.03547
ladder.note: A simpler sieve that tracks the density of the uncovered set; part (b) closes Selfridge's route to an odd covering via moduli none of which divides another.

ladder.title: Every distinct covering has a modulus divisible by 2 or 3
ladder.q: Prove that in every distinct covering system (distinct moduli, all greater than 1, covering $\mathbb Z$) at least one modulus is divisible by $2$ or by $3$.
ladder.source: R. D. Hough and P. P. Nielsen, Covering systems with restricted divisibility, Duke Math. J. 168 (2019); arXiv:1703.02133
ladder.note: The strongest unconditional step towards the odd covering problem: an odd covering would need a modulus divisible by 3.

ladder.title: No odd square-free distinct covering
ladder.q: Prove that if a finite set of congruences $x\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ with distinct square-free moduli $n_i>1$ covers $\mathbb Z$, then at least one $n_i$ is even.
ladder.source: P. Balister, B. Bollobás, R. Morris, J. Sahasrabudhe and M. Tiba, The Erdős–Selfridge problem with square-free moduli, Algebra Number Theory 15 (2021); arXiv:1901.11465
ladder.note: Settles the square-free case of the Erdős–Selfridge odd covering problem; the general odd case remains open.

ladder.title: Primitive subsets of {1, ..., 2n}
ladder.q:
A set $A$ of positive integers is primitive if no element of $A$ divides another element of $A$.

Prove that for every $n\ge1$ the largest primitive subset of $\{1,2,\ldots,2n\}$ has exactly $n$ elements.
ladder.source: Folklore (Erdős); see M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, chapter Pigeon-hole and double counting
ladder.note: Grouping by odd part gives the upper bound and $\{n+1,\ldots,2n\}$ the lower bound: counting alone cannot force primitive sets to be thin, which is why weighted sums are used.

ladder.title: Erdős's disjoint-multiples inequality
ladder.q:
For an integer $a\ge2$ let $P(a)$ be its largest prime factor and let $S_a$ be the set of integers $am$ with $m\ge1$ and every prime factor of $m$ at least $P(a)$.

Let $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ be primitive. Prove that the sets $S_a$ ($a\in A$) are pairwise disjoint, that $S_a$ has natural density $\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}\left(1-\frac1p\right)$ (product over primes), and deduce $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\prod_{p<P(a)}\left(1-\frac1p\right)\le1.$$
ladder.source: P. Erdős, Note on sequences of integers no one of which is divisible by any other, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 126–128
ladder.note: The key inequality in Erdős's 1935 argument; the rest is Mertens' theorem.

ladder.title: Erdős: the sum of 1/(a log a) is uniformly bounded
ladder.q:
Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}\le C.$$

Deduce that every primitive set has lower asymptotic density $0$.
ladder.source: P. Erdős, Note on sequences of integers no one of which is divisible by any other, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 126–128
ladder.note: Mertens' estimate $\prod_{p<y}(1-1/p)\asymp1/\log y$ applied to the previous rung; the primes show the sum can be about 1.6366, and the research problem asks whether that is the maximum.

ladder.title: Besicovitch: primitive sets can have positive upper density
ladder.q: Prove that there exists a primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ with positive upper asymptotic density, i.e. $$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x}>0.$$
ladder.source: A. S. Besicovitch, On the density of certain sequences of integers, Math. Ann. 110 (1934/35), 336-341
ladder.note: Shows the previous rung cannot be upgraded to natural density zero; equivalently, sets of multiples need not have a natural density, which is why the Davenport–Erdős theory uses logarithmic density.

ladder.title: Davenport–Erdős: sets of multiples have logarithmic density
ladder.q:
Let $A$ be a set of positive integers and let $M(A)=\{am: a\in A,\ m\ge1\}$ be its set of multiples.

Prove that $M(A)$ has a logarithmic density, i.e. $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac1{\log x}\sum_{n\in M(A),\,n\le x}\frac1n$ exists, and that it equals the lower asymptotic density of $M(A)$.
ladder.source: H. Davenport and P. Erdős, On sequences of positive integers, Acta Arith. 2 (1936), 147-151; elementary proof in J. Indian Math. Soc. (N.S.) 15 (1951), 19-24
ladder.note: The case $X_n=\{0\}$ of Erdős Problem 486; the open problem asks the same for an arbitrary choice of forbidden residues $X_n$.

ladder.title: Behrend's bound for reciprocal sums
ladder.q: Prove that there is an absolute constant $C$ such that for all $x\ge3$ and every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\lfloor x\rfloor\}$, $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\le C\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}.$$
ladder.source: F. Behrend, On sequences of numbers not divisible one by another, J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935)
ladder.note: In particular primitive sets have logarithmic density zero; the real-number analogue of this bound is part of Erdős Problem 143.

ladder.title: The e^gamma bound
ladder.q: Prove that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}<e^{\gamma}=1.78107\ldots,$$ where $\gamma$ is Euler's constant.
ladder.source: J. D. Lichtman and C. Pomerance, The Erdős conjecture for primitive sets, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B 6 (2019), 1-14; arXiv:1806.02250
ladder.note: Brings the universal bound within about 9 percent of the conjectured extremal value $\sum_p 1/(p\log p)=1.6366\ldots$.

ladder.title: Lichtman: the primes maximise the Erdős sum
ladder.q: Prove that every primitive set $A\subseteq\{2,3,\ldots\}$ satisfies $$\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}\le\sum_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\frac1{p\log p}.$$
ladder.source: J. D. Lichtman, A proof of the Erdős primitive set conjecture, Forum Math. Pi 11 (2023); arXiv:2202.02384
ladder.note: Resolves Erdős's conjecture; the translated version for primitive sets in $[x,\infty)$ and the real-number analogue are the next questions.
